entries.answer: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea, and it is the word every other part of a sentence can point at. What separates a proper noun from a common one is not the kind of thing but whether it identifies a particular instance, so Jordan names one river while river names any of them. Abstract nouns cause the most trouble for learners, because freedom is a noun even though nothing can be pointed at, and people often reach for a clumsier word instead.

entries.answer: An adjective modifies a noun or pronoun, usually by describing some quality, and English puts it before the noun as in a red car. The other position sits after the verb, where it describes the subject rather than the noun, as in the car stopped red. Only a small set can do both, and those are the ones worth learning by heart, because the position changes the meaning rather than the grammar.

entries.answer: An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb, which makes it the most flexible word class in English. The three positions it can occupy are all real and all change emphasis, since she quietly closed the door and she closed the door quietly carry the same facts but draw attention differently. Adverbs of manner, degree, time and place are separate categories, and the ending -ly covers only some of them.

entries.answer: Two words are synonyms when they share a meaning without sharing every shade of it, which is why dictionaries print graded lists rather than tidy pairs. Deep and profound overlap, but one suits a well and the other suits an idea, and choosing wrongly is usually a register error rather than a meaning error. The practical test is whether a sentence built on the swap still sounds like the same speaker.

entries.answer: An antonym is a word with an opposite meaning, and not every opposite is a true antonym, because some are merely complements. Hot and cold invert each other, but wet and dry are simply the two ends of one scale, and a learner hunting for a neat rule trips over pairs like borrow and lend, which invert roles rather than meanings. A good antonym is also gradable, so the opposite of big is small and the opposite of beautiful is ugly.

entries.answer: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its parts, so let it alone means do not touch it and also means stop interfering. Idioms are stored whole in memory rather than assembled on the spot, which is exactly why they often seem arbitrary. The productive ones follow patterns, and the group worth watching is the phrasal verbs, where a particle changes the verb entirely as in give up, give in and give out.

entries.answer: A collocation is a pairing that sounds natural to a native speaker and wrong when translated word for word, and it is the most visible mark of a non-native writer. The individual words are correct, they simply do not belong together, so British English prefers the machine was being repaired where American English prefers fixed. Learning collocations beats learning rules here, because you are memorising a finished phrase rather than deriving one.
